fields.title: Economics at Different Scales
fields.keyTakeaway: Unit cost at a tenfold scale shows whether the economics are healthy, and only this check reveals superlinear items and thresholds in advance.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: A solution that is cheap with a thousand users — will it be cheap with a million?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Architectural decisions are evaluated at the current scale, but they live until the next one. A decision whose cost grows faster than revenue shows up as a problem a year or two later, when rewriting it costs a quarter.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: Three types of cost behavior during growth.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Sublinear.** Cost grows slower than volume. Fixed costs are spread out, economies of scale work. A sign of a healthy architecture.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Linear.** Cost is proportional to volume. Neutral, but does not improve margin as growth happens. Typical for external services with a per-unit price.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Superlinear.** Cost grows faster than volume. Concerning. Causes:
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: *Data accumulation.* Grows as the integral of the inflow. *Operations depending on total volume.* A query scanning the entire table gets more expensive as the table grows — even with a constant number of queries. *Entity relationships.* A network with N users can have up to N² connections. *Coordination.* More services and teams mean more overhead.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: Practical check: **calculate the unit cost now and at tenfold volume.** If it is growing, find the cause now, not later.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: A separate case is **thresholds.** Cost can be linear up to a certain point and jump up: transition to sharding, to another pricing tier, to another architecture. Thresholds from `PF2-N4-L2` are the same thing, but viewed from the money side.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Storage is the only superlinear item, and the reason is clear: accumulation. Retention keeps it in check, but does not cancel it.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: The total is nearly linear, meaning the economies of scale are eaten up by data accumulation. This is not a catastrophe, but it means the margin will not improve automatically with growth.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: Thresholds ahead: database sharding (already in the plan), analytics pricing tier, acquiring limit of 200 transactions per second — at tenfold growth the peak will be 150, which is close to the limit.
fields.sections/3/blocks/5/text: The last one is the most useful finding: the contract with the provider needs to be renegotiated a year before we hit the limit.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: A tenfold extrapolation is rough and does not account for changes in the product profile. It answers the question "is there a structural problem" rather than providing a forecast.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Unit cost at a tenfold scale shows whether the economics are healthy, and only this check reveals superlinear items and thresholds in advance.
